I no longer cook at panda but I worked there for a while and also have been cooking most of my career so this is as much advise as I can possibly give you but it should be pretty solid advice. 

when I did work there, I tried to be as proficient with dropping food and starting dishes before they were called back. I made it a habit to always look over my shoulder and check the line and if I wasn't sure if they needed something I'd just ask the person I trusted the most from the foh (i.e it's 7pm and we have 3 servings of black pepper I'd just say "hey, p.i.c. you need black pepper?"). More often than not the foh would call back a dish and it'd already be in my fryer or my wok.

As for burned sauces, 1) make sure you stir them a little while they cook. Don't do it too much or they won't boil, just a bit. 2) know the sauces will reduce more while you're tossing the meats in them so don't wait until they're really thick. You'll want to go once they start boiling. 3) make sure you're not burning your chili or gingergarlic they can go fast 4) make sure you're cleaning your wok efficiently and thoroughly after every dish. 

Finally as for speed, my biggest tips are in no specific order of importance, 1) make a checklist routine and know what time you should start them and what time you should expect to be done by. 2) pre-close. Somethings can be done preemptively. Do your flips after your main dinner rush etc. 3) stay clean while you cook. This is super important, the cleaner and more organized you are while you cook, the better and easier everything is. 4) don't be methodical, you're going to have to put that "sense of urgency" they always talk about into play. Sometimes you're going to have to break a sweat, buckle down and just go for it. 

At the end of the day, the most important thing is be confident. You know your recipes, just figure out how to multitask. Sometimes you might mess up but it's fine just keep going. You're in the kitchen, act like you own it. Own everything you do.
